question: What does an antenna (aerial) do?

options.text: Radiates radio energy, or receives it
Adds audio information to the carrier
Amplifies the signal in the receiver
Converts the carrier to audio frequency

explanation: The aerial is the interface between the equipment and space: it radiates energy from a transmitter and collects it for a receiver. Its type depends on the job — omnidirectional voice, a narrow radar beam, a direction-finding loop and so on.

question: Which two basic aerials are used for ordinary transmission and reception?

options.text: The slotted array and the helical aerial
The Yagi array and the horn feed
The half-wave dipole and quarter-wave Marconi
The loop aerial and the parabolic dish reflector

explanation: The half-wave dipole and the quarter-wave Marconi aerial are the basic types. The others are specialised: loops for direction finding, dishes and slotted arrays for radar.

question: Where is power fed into a half-wave dipole, and in what direction does it radiate best?

options.text: At the centre; most strongly along the line of the aerial
At the centre; most strongly at right angles to the aerial
At one end; equally in all directions including the ends
At one end; most strongly along the line of the aerial

explanation: A dipole is fed at its centre and radiates perpendicular to its length, with no radiation off its ends.

question: How does a quarter-wave Marconi aerial work as half of a dipole?

options.text: It uses the ionosphere as a reflector to form the other half
It is folded back on itself to double its electrical length
It is joined to a second Marconi aerial on the opposite side of the aircraft
It stands, insulated, on a metal surface that forms the other half

explanation: The Marconi aerial is mounted on a conducting surface (an aircraft's skin), which acts as the "mirror" second half of a dipole. Radiation is perpendicular to the aerial.

question: Why are Marconi (quarter-wave) aerials normally used on aircraft?

options.text: They work equally well on every frequency band
They are short and aerodynamically better
They radiate only upwards, away from ground clutter and reflections
They need no connection to the aircraft's metal skin

explanation: Half the length of a dipole and mounted directly on the fuselage, a quarter-wave aerial gives far less drag — hence the short blade aerials on aircraft.

question: What is the ideal electrical length of a quarter-wave aerial for 150 MHz?

options.text: 1 m
25 cm
2 m
50 cm

explanation: λ = 300 / 150 = 2 m, and a quarter of that is 0.5 m = 50 cm. A half-wave dipole for the same frequency would be 1 m.

question: What is the ideal electrical length of a half-wave dipole for 100 MHz?

options.text: 3 m

explanation: λ = 300 / 100 = 3 m, so half a wavelength is 1.5 m. A quarter-wave aerial would be 0.75 m.

question: Why is a real aerial made slightly shorter than its theoretical half- or quarter-wavelength?

options.text: Shortening the aerial removes the unwanted side lobes
A shorter aerial produces less sky-wave interference
The wave travels more slowly in the conductor
The aircraft's speed shortens the effective wavelength

explanation: Electromagnetic energy slows in a denser medium, so the wavelength inside the conductor is a little shorter than in free space. Aerial lengths are cut a few percent short to allow for it.

question: What is the theoretical length of a quarter-wave aerial for 406 MHz?

options.text: About 74 cm
About 37 cm
About 9.2 cm
About 18.5 cm

explanation: λ = 300 / 406 ≈ 0.739 m, and a quarter is about 0.185 m = 18.5 cm. In practice the aerial is cut a few percent shorter, because the wave travels more slowly in the conductor.

question: What is the theoretical length of a half-wave dipole for 75 MHz?

options.text: 4 m
2 m
1 m

explanation: λ = 300 / 75 = 4 m, so a half-wave dipole is 2 m (in practice a little shorter).

question: What connects an aerial to its transmitter or receiver at UHF?

options.text: Coaxial cable
A simple single wire
A hollow waveguide
A twin-wire feeder

explanation: Feeder losses rise with frequency. A single wire is fine at LF/MF, twin wire suits HF and VHF, coaxial cable is needed at UHF, and a waveguide takes over in the upper UHF, SHF and EHF bands.

question: Which feeder is adequate at LF and MF?

options.text: A waveguide
A twin-wire feeder
A simple wire
A coaxial cable

explanation: At low and medium frequencies losses are small, so a simple wire carries the signal over reasonable distances.

question: What is a waveguide?

options.text: A metal rod placed in front of an aerial to focus its beam
A hollow rectangular metal tube that carries the energy
A ferrite core inside a direction-finding loop aerial
A coaxial cable with a solid copper inner conductor

explanation: In the upper UHF, SHF and EHF bands, cable and simple aerials lose too much energy, so the energy is carried inside a hollow metal tube.

question: How are the internal dimensions of a waveguide related to the frequency it carries?

options.text: They are unrelated to the frequency
They are about twice the wavelength
They are about a quarter of the wavelength
They are about half the wavelength

explanation: The waveguide's internal size is set at about half the wavelength in use, which is why waveguides are practical only at very short (centimetric) wavelengths.

question: What does an aerial's polar diagram show?

options.text: The path the signal takes through the ionosphere
The aerial's output power plotted against each frequency used
A line joining points of equal signal strength
The phase of the signal at each distance

explanation: A polar diagram plots equal signal strength round an aerial, normally as a plan view of the plane of radiation. The same pattern applies to reception.

question: What three-dimensional shape is the radiation pattern of a simple dipole?

options.text: A torus (ring) centred on the aerial
A sphere centred on the aerial
A figure-of-eight in every plane
A cone pointing away from the feed point of the aerial

explanation: Radiation is strongest at right angles to the dipole and zero off its ends, so the 3-D pattern is a ring (torus) round the aerial — omnidirectional in the plane at right angles to it.

question: How can a simple aerial be made directional?

options.text: By using a lower frequency for the same aerial length
By adding parasitic elements: reflector and directors
By changing it from vertical to horizontal polarization
By feeding it from one end instead of feeding it from the centre

explanation: The simplest way is to add unpowered (parasitic) elements: a reflector behind and directors in front. The familiar television aerial is built this way.

question: How is a reflector element sized and placed relative to a dipole?

options.text: About 5% longer, a half-wavelength in front of it
About 5% shorter, a half-wavelength in front of it
About 5% longer, a quarter-wavelength behind it
The same length, a full wavelength behind it

explanation: A rod about 5% longer than the aerial, a quarter-wavelength away in the same plane, re-radiates out of phase so there is no signal behind it and a stronger signal in front.

question: Compared with the aerial, how big are director elements?

options.text: Exactly the same length
Larger than the aerial
5% longer than the reflector
Smaller than the aerial

explanation: Directors are slightly shorter than the driven aerial and sit in front of it, focusing energy into a stronger forward beam.

question: What is the main drawback of making an aerial directional?

options.text: Unwanted side lobes
It needs a higher frequency band to work at all
Reversed polarization
It always reduces the range

explanation: A strong main beam comes with side lobes that also transmit and receive. They cause "ghosting" on TV, and give real problems in SSR, ILS and primary radar.

question: How does an ILS localizer aerial form its narrow beams?

options.text: A loop aerial producing a figure-of-eight pattern
A rotating parabolic dish fed by a waveguide
A line of 16 or 24 aerials, half a wavelength apart
A single dipole with one reflector a quarter-wavelength behind it

explanation: The localizer array uses many elements in a line, fed so that two narrow, symmetrical lobes form either side of the runway centre line.

question: What causes "ghosting" on a television picture?

options.text: The reflector being too far behind the aerial
Sky waves arriving from the ionosphere at night
The transmitter changing its polarization
Reflected signals received in the aerial's side lobes

explanation: Directional arrays have side lobes that pick up signals reflected from buildings, producing a delayed second image. The same side-lobe problem affects SSR, ILS and primary radar.

question: In which aviation systems are side lobes a major problem that must be addressed?

options.text: SSR and ILS, and also primary radar
VOR and HF communications
NDB and VDF
Marker beacons only

explanation: Side lobes give false indications in SSR and ILS and false echoes in primary radar, so these systems include measures to suppress or ignore them.

question: Which aerial is used to sense the direction of an incoming signal in an ADF?

options.text: A slotted array
A loop aerial
A parabolic dish
A Marconi aerial

explanation: An ADF uses a loop aerial whose output depends on its orientation to the incoming wave.

question: When does a loop aerial give zero output?

options.text: When it is tuned exactly to the transmitter's frequency
When its plane is at right angles to the incoming wave
When the signal is horizontally polarized
When its plane is aligned with the incoming wave

explanation: Square to the wave, both vertical sides of the loop receive the signal in phase, the induced currents are equal and cancel: a null. Aligned with the wave, there is a phase difference and a net current flows.

question: What polar diagram does a loop aerial produce?

options.text: A narrow pencil beam with side lobes
A circle with no nulls
A figure-of-eight with two nulls
A cardioid with one null

explanation: A loop gives a figure-of-eight pattern with two sharp nulls. The nulls are used to find direction, but having two of them creates a 180° ambiguity that an ADF must resolve.

question: In which frequency bands do radar systems operate?

options.text: LF and MF
HF and VHF
VHF and UHF
UHF and SHF

explanation: Radars use UHF and SHF. At these frequencies the energy is carried by waveguide rather than cable.

question: Where is the waveguide feed placed in a parabolic dish aerial?

options.text: At the focus of the parabola
At the rim of the dish
At twice the focal length
Behind the centre of the dish, facing forwards

explanation: Placing the open waveguide at the focus makes every path from feed to dish to wavefront the same length, so the reflected energy leaves as parallel rays, all in phase.

question: What does a parabolic reflector do to the energy from its feed?

options.text: Turns linear polarization into circular polarization
Spreads the energy evenly in all directions
Turns a point source into an in-phase plane wavefront
Converts a plane wavefront into a point source

explanation: The dish turns the spreading energy from its focus into a plane wavefront. In theory a pencil beam results; in practice it diverges except very close to the dish.

question: Why does a parabolic dish produce side lobes?

options.text: The waveguide is half a wavelength wide
Uneven reflection spills energy outside the beam
The feed is placed exactly at the focal point
The dish converts the signal to circular polarization

explanation: Some energy is reflected unevenly and spills from the reflector. These side lobes can be strong enough to give real echoes from outside the main beam.

question: What is a flat plate (slotted, phased array) antenna?

options.text: A flat plate with many slots, each fed from behind
A loop aerial wound on a flat ferrite core
A row of 24 dipoles with half-wavelength spacing on a mast
A flat metal reflector with a waveguide horn at its focus

explanation: The beam is formed by the interaction of many small beams from slots cut in the plate. It is now the usual design for airborne weather radar.

question: Which is an advantage of a flat plate (slotted) array over a parabolic dish?

options.text: Longer pulses for better range
Wider beam for the same frequency
More power needed for the same range
Reduced side lobes

explanation: The flat plate array wastes less energy in side lobes and concentrates it into a narrower beam, so it needs less power for a given range. It also allows a narrower pulse and improved resolution.

question: Which list gives the advantages of a flat plate array over a parabolic reflector?

options.text: Narrower beam, larger side lobes, less power, longer pulse
Narrower beam, fewer side lobes, less power, finer resolution
Wider beam, smaller side lobes, more power, much longer range
Wider beam, larger side lobes, more power, better resolution

explanation: Narrow beam, reduced side lobes, less power for a given range, narrower pulse and improved resolution are the standard list.

question: Does a parabolic reflector produce a perfectly parallel pencil beam at all ranges?

options.text: No; apart from close to the aerial, the beam diverges
No; it converges to a point at the focal length
Yes; it stays the same width at all ranges
Yes; but only for horizontally polarized energy

explanation: In principle the reflected rays are parallel, but in practice the beam spreads out except very near the dish.
